node.label: Patrick Wolfe
node.date_label: Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology 1999 · later essays 2001, 2006 · coverage through 2000
node.description: Reads the history of anthropology through settler colonialism. Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) studies virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse, and Victorian anthropology on mother-right, totemism and E. B. Tylor. Later essays address land, labour and race (2001) and the elimination of the native (2006).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Patrick Wolfe (1949–2016); Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology: The Politics and Poetics of an Ethnographic Event (1999). Later readings: “Land, Labor, and Difference: Elementary Structures of Race” (2001); “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006).
node.scope_note: This entry presents the 1999 book. Its introduction (pp. 1–2, read) distinguishes settler from franchise colonies, holds that settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies' and states that 'invasion is a structure not an event'; the rest of the book is checked at contents and catalogue level. The 2001 and 2006 essays are later readings. He did not originate the term, which has earlier usage (Veracini 2013), and he is not presented as the field's founder.

proposed_edges.relationship: Settler colonialism as the frame for a history of anthropology (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The 1999 book names settler colonialism in its title. Its contents page titles the introduction 'Text and Context: Anthropology and Settler Colonialism' and chapter 1 'White Man's Flour: Virgin Birth in Anthropology and in Australian Settler Discourse'; chapter 2 is 'Science, Colonialism and Anthropology: The Logic of a Global Transformation'. Library subject headings add Australian frontier life, imperialism and racism in anthropology. Introduction pp. 1–2 read: settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies' and 'invasion is a structure not an event'. The rest of the book is checked at contents and catalogue level. A contribution, not a founding: earlier settler-society studies (1983, 1995) and earlier usage of the term (Veracini 2013) precede it. In the sampled corpus, 17 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book (earliest observed citation 2012) and 54 cite any of his works; the citation share rises from 1.0% (2009–14) to 8.6% (2020–26). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. The 2006 essay is a later reading, not evidence for this edge.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No strand target proposed. settler_colonialism/structure_and_elimination holds Wolfe and the 1999 book, but its focus is the 'structure, not event' formulation, which is not checked in the 1999 book here. Targeting it would imply that check.

proposed_edges.relationship: A history of Victorian and Australian anthropology in its settler-colonial setting
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1999). The contents page lists chapters on mother-right ('Sex and Property in Victorian Anthropology'), totemism ('Victorian Anthropology's Eternal Dichotomy') and E. B. Tylor ('Survival in a Paradigm Shift: E.B. Tylor and the Problem of the Text'), alongside virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse. Catalogue subjects: Anthropology -- Australia -- History; Racism in anthropology -- Australia. Introduction p. 1 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements'. The chapters' stance toward these anthropologists is not read here. If the introduction confirms a critical argument, a critique edge to anthropology/evolution may be the better reading. A historian's account of the discipline, not anthropological fieldwork.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: colonial_knowledge ('Knowledge, authority and historical categories') fits a study of how anthropological categories took shape under colonial conditions. The evolution strand names Tylor, but a contribution edge there would read as a contribution to evolutionism.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not warranted. The only in-period work is the 1999 book. Its contents treat anthropological and settler representations (virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse, 'Repressive Authenticity'); catalogue subjects include 'Australian aborigines -- Public opinion'. That is a history of settler and anthropological knowledge, not a contribution to Indigenous historical practice, community authority or decolonizing method. The Indigenous entry's scope says neither anthropology nor European theory is the common origin of these practices. The relation is already carried by the roster comparison row (ind127_wolfe_1999), its strand settler_colonial_interlocutor and edge_881 (indigenous — settler_colonialism comparison). Indigenous engagement with his theory (Kauanui 2016; Konishi 2019) is post-2000 and runs partly as critique; it belongs in the settler colonialism entry.

Evidence is the 2001 and 2016 works, after 2000, and title level only. edge_885 (settler_colonialism — racial_formation comparison) already carries it. Defer to an extension release that registers works and claims.

verification.note: Publisher preview PDF reproducing the 1999 Cassell edition (imprint page: 'First published 1999', ISBNs 0-304-70339-7 and 0-304-70340-0). Pages 1–2 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements' in the development of Australian settler colonialism; postcolonial theory works with 'an oddly monolithic ... notion of colonialism'; settler colonies 'were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour' but are premised on displacing indigenes from the land; 'Settler colonies were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies ... The colonizers come to stay - invasion is a structure not an event' (p. 2). Later pages not read here.
